Compile-Time Tensor Shape Checking via Staged Shape-Dependent Types
Takashi Suwa, Atsushi Igarashi

Abstract
When writing programs involving matrices or tensors in general, it is desirable to rule out the inconsistency of tensor shapes (i.e., the generalization of matrix sizes) before actual computation. For this purpose, some languages provide dependent types such as 𝙼𝚊𝚝 ​ m ​ n \mathtt{Mat}\ m\ n , and others offer refinement types to track predicates for shapes. Despite the theoretical maturity, however, such methods are often unhandy for continuous software development due to the requirement of proofs for judging type equality or subtyping; even automated proving is often unsuitable due to its unforeseeable time consumption. To remedy this, our study provides an alternative formalization by using staging . Based on the observation that conditions for the shape consistency can be extracted before running the actual tensor computations in many typical cases, we ensure such consistency by assertions evaluated as compile-time computations, not by proofs. Under this formalization, we can verify the consistency virtually statically in the sense that inconsistencies will be immediately detected as failures during compile-time computation. Our work achieves a mathematical guarantee that successfully generated code is always consistent with respect to tensor shapes. Furthermore, to vastly lessen the burden of adding shape- or stage-related descriptions, we (1) allow shape-related arguments to be implicit and infer them in a best-effort manner, and (2) offer a non-staged surface language that seemingly resembles ordinary dependently-typed languages and translate its programs into the staged core language. By a prototype implementation, we confirm that our language is expressive enough to verify a number of programs, including several examples offered by ocaml-torch .

1
Introduction

1.1
Background: Tensor Computation and Shape Checking

Nowadays,
tensors
or
multi-dimensional arrays

(i.e., vectors, matrices, cuboids, and so on)
are nearly everywhere;
they have long been used in various methods for mathematical optimization,
and recently, due to the growing demand for machine learning,
tensors have been intensively used
to represent various structures related to deep neural networks (DNN).

When it comes to writing programs involving tensors,
it is desirable to rule out the inconsistency of
tensor shapes

(i.e., the generalization of vector lengths or matrix sizes)
before running actual computations.
For example, consider the function
f
that
takes three matrices
A
,
B
, and
C
and computes
A(B\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}C\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}B)
,
where
\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}
is a binary operator that vertically concatenates two matrices.
For verifying consistency, the following constraints must be met:
(1) for the use of
\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}
,

B
and
C
must have the same number of columns; and
(2) for the matrix multiplication,
the number of
A
’s columns must be equal to
the number of
(B\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}C\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}B)
’s rows.
Checking such constraints during program execution is problematic because it may cause
a runtime error due to some trifling shape mismatch bugs only after heavy computations,
consuming much time.

A popular approach to addressing this kind of problem is to use dependent type systems.
Some languages, such as Idris
[
7
,
8
]
,
provide dependent types like
\mathtt{Vec}\ n
or
\mathtt{Mat}\ m\ n
,
which are the type for vectors of length
n
and
the one for matrices of size
m\times n
, respectively, and assign
the matrix multiplication the following type:

\forall p,q,r:\mathtt{Nat}.\ \mathtt{Mat}\ p\ q\to\mathtt{Mat}\ q\ r\to\mathtt{Mat}\ p\ r
.
Other methods,
such as
GraTen
[
33
]
,
offer refinement types like

\{\nu:\mathtt{Tensor}\mid\nu.\mathtt{shape}=[m,n]\}

or

\{\nu:\mathtt{Tensor}\mid\mathtt{len}(\nu.\mathtt{shape})=3\}
.
As an example of this kind of approach,
consider the function
f
above implemented in an Idris-like hypothetical language:

\displaystyle\mathbf{lemma}\ \mathit{HeightsMatch}\ k\ m:m+k+m=k+2\ast m\ \mathbf{proof}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{end}

\displaystyle\mathbf{let}\ f\ \{j:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{k:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{m:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{n:\mathtt{Nat}\}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\hskip 10.00002pt\ (A:\mathtt{Mat}\ j\ (k+2\ast m))\ (B:\mathtt{Mat}\ m\ n)\ (C:\mathtt{Mat}\ k\ n)=

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathbf{let}\ D=\mathit{vertCat}\ (\mathit{vertCat}\ B\ C)\ B\ \mathbf{in}\ \mathit{matMult}\ A\ (\mathbf{rewrite}\ \mathit{HeightsMatch}\ k\ m\ \mathbf{in}\ D)

Here,
\{j:\mathtt{Nat}\}\cdots\{n:\mathtt{Nat}\}
are binders for implicit parameters, and

\mathit{matMult}
and
\mathit{vertCat}

stand for the matrix multiplication and
\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}
,
which are assigned
types
\forall p,q,r:\mathtt{Nat}.\ \mathtt{Mat}\ p\ q\to\mathtt{Mat}\ q\ r\to\mathtt{Mat}\ p\ r

and
\forall p,q,r:\mathtt{Nat}.\ \mathtt{Mat}\ p\ r\to\mathtt{Mat}\ q\ r\to\mathtt{Mat}\ (p+q)\ r
,
respectively.

\mathit{HeightsMatch}\ k\ m
is a manually proved lemma used for
matching
D
’s actual type with the one required of
D
;
since
D
is of type
\mathtt{Mat}\ (m+k+m)\ n

and the function
(\mathit{matMult}\ A)
requires its argument to be of
\mathtt{Mat}\ (k+2\ast m)\ r^{\prime}

for some
r^{\prime}
, the type-checker must verify that
m+k+m=k+2\ast m
holds.
Working as a proof, the lemma rewrites the former type to the latter
through the
\mathbf{rewrite}
-construct.
In general, to type-check an application
M_{1}\ M_{2}
,
where
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
are known to have
types
\mathtt{Mat}\ M^{\prime}_{11}\ M^{\prime}_{12}\to T
and
\mathtt{Mat}\ M^{\prime}_{21}\ M^{\prime}_{22}
,
respectively,
we must prove the type equality
\mathtt{Mat}\ M^{\prime}_{11}\ M^{\prime}_{12}=\mathtt{Mat}\ M^{\prime}_{21}\ M^{\prime}_{22}
,
i.e., that, for
i\in\{1,2\}
,

argument expressions

M^{\prime}_{1i}
and
M^{\prime}_{2i}
always describe
the same value in the given context.
Languages of such approaches provide some form of mechanism for proving this equality.

Despite their theoretic maturity and success in many safety-critical fields, however,
such verification methods do not seem to be so eagerly applied to
relatively typical,
continuous
software development, especially cases in industry.
Although various reasons can be considered for this,
we suppose that the following situations would be major factors:

1.

The externality of requirements
:
Requirements imposed on software continuously arise due to
social situations and users’ preferences,
which are not predictable beforehand.

2.

The sequential nature of software development
:
Checking is performed repeatedly during development.
Although we can restrict properties to check to some lightweight ones
for frequently performed verification,
it would still be better if we do not have to take much time for each run,
in order not to harm productivity.

3.

Time is literally money
:
It is costly to let software engineers engaged in development.
Moreover, each engineer is available for approximately only 40 hours per week.

Under such circumstances,
major issues that hamper adoption of existing methods for tensor shape checking
would be some of the following:

A.

Cumbersomeness of future changes
:
Methods that require manual proving easily make
future changes of programs unwieldy;
even slight modification of programs may demand nearly complete amendment of proofs.
This does not go along with the condition 1 above,
i.e., the unpredictable nature of requirements imposed on software.

B.

Unpredictable time consumption by automated proving
:
To reduce the burden of manual proving,
some methods provide automated proving by using back-end solvers,
possibly with some part of the syntax restricted to a subset suitable for automation.
However, such approaches are often too time-consuming or at least take unpredictable time;
slight change of properties to check may drastically increase the elapsed time.

C.

Frequent false-positive errors
:
As pointed out in some articles like Ascari et al.
[
4
]

or a CACM article about the use of static analyses
in Facebook (currently known as Meta)
[
20
]
,
methods for verifying detailed properties are likely to cause false positives too easily
due to their nature of the overapproximation of program behaviors.
Namely, even when the validity is clear for humans,
analysis tools often warn, e.g., the existence of a type-level gap
and require some form of annotations or proofs.
Frequent false-positive errors also add additional cumbersomeness to future changes
1
1

1

“Theoreticians,” including the authors,
tend to take false-positive errors for granted
(since we cannot achieve sound and complete verification
and thereby overapproximations of some kind are necessarily introduced).
However, for an affinity with development workflows,
it would even be worth considering to strike a balance
between soundness properties and the frequency of false positives.

.

D.

Lack of concise support for flexible tensor-handling operations
:
There are some implicit conversions of tensors
frequently utilized in DNN-related programs,
such as
broadcasting

[
19
,
14
]
.
These conversions are flexible enough to make reasoning tensor shapes non-trivial,
at least beyond decidable theories.
For example,
two tensors of shapes
[5, 3, 1, 10]
and
[3, 4, 10]
are
addable by broadcasting
(specifically, by duplicating the former by
4
along with the third dimension
and the latter by
5
, respectively).
Typical type systems have difficulty in supporting such conversions
in a concise manner; they will require proofs for
the feasibility of the conversion, and whether the proving is
manual or automated, that will also lead to some of the issues A–C above.

In essence, for the adoption to continuous development,
it would also be crucial to wipe off the concern about
the burden arising from the mismatch between verification methods and development workflows,
such as the one due to too many false positives or unpredictable time consumption,
not only to establish a method to verify the correctness of programs.

1.2
Basics of Our Language Design

To mitigate the issues A–D above for tensor-manipulating programs,
this work provides an alternative formalization of tensor shape checking
by using
staging
(also called
staged computation
or
multi-stage programming

[
16
,
17
,
67
,
68
]
).
Our key idea is to split tensor computation into two stages: the stage
0
,
which can be regarded as compile-time,
is to verify
the shape consistency by
assertion checking
and generate a specialized program which is
proven not to cause any run-time shape mismatch; and the stage
1
is to do actual tensor computation by
the specialized program.
Our method is based on the observation
2
2

2

Though our formalization may be general enough to be applied to other topics,
we have not found other usages that fit this kind of phase separation
and thereby focus on tensor shape checking for now.

that, in many tensor-manipulating programs, especially
the ones that use sophisticated tensor libraries,
the computation to check shape consistency can be independent of the actual tensor computations
and thus is expected to be lightweight.
Let us discuss the core of our idea using a concrete example.
The previous example can be expressed as the following staged program
3
3

3

Notes to those who are not very familiar to multi-stage programs:
We use the notations from
MetaML

[
67
,
68
]
.
Here, expressions of the
forms
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
(called
bracket
)
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M}
(called
escape
)
correspond to (hygienic)
quasiquotation
and
splicing
in Lisp, respectively.
Intuitively, a bracket
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

evaluates to a code value: for example,

\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}1}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}4}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
evaluates to itself,
which stands for a piece of code that performs addition of 1 and 4.
An escape
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M}
is supposed to appear inside a bracket;
when
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M}
is evaluated to a code value
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\prime}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
,
the code
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\prime}}
is spliced into the surrounding code:
For example,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{a}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{1}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{4}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{in}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{a}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
evaluates to
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\ast}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{1}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{4}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.
The symbol
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}
(called
cross-stage persistence

[
32
,
42
,
67
,
77
]

in the literature) signifies that
the argument comes from a lower stage.
Unlike escapes, the argument can be of any type.

:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{A}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\hskip 10.00002pt{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{D}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}=}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathbf{in}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\hskip 10.00002pt{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{A}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{D}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

We use blue and orange to render stage-0 and stage-1 entities, respectively, throughout the paper
4
4

4

Nonetheless, for accessibility reasons, we do not disambiguate stages just by colors.

.
Numerous shape-related arguments are used in the program for now,
but one can see later that many of them can actually be implicit.

Basically,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
takes

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}

as stage-
0
parameters,
and produces code for
(A,B,C)\mapsto A(B\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}C\mathbin{\text{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.99994pt}{\footnotesize$+$}\hss}}\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{\footnotesize$+$}}B)

specialized for those parameters.
Here,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
takes
three parameters
\mathtt{\mathit{p}}
,
\mathtt{\mathit{q}}
, and
\mathtt{\mathit{r}}

and returns
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}_{\mathtt{\mathit{p}},\mathtt{\mathit{q}},\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
, where

{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}_{\mathtt{\mathit{p}},\mathtt{\mathit{q}},\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}}
is
the specialized operation that vertically concatenates

\mathtt{\mathit{p}}\times\mathtt{\mathit{r}}
and
\mathtt{\mathit{q}}\times\mathtt{\mathit{r}}
matrices.
The stage-
0
built-in function
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
also takes
three parameters
\mathtt{\mathit{p}}
,
\mathtt{\mathit{q}}
, and
\mathtt{\mathit{r}}

and returns
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}_{\mathtt{\mathit{p}},\mathtt{\mathit{q}},\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
, where

{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}_{\mathtt{\mathit{p}},\mathtt{\mathit{q}},\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}}
is the matrix multiplication operation
specialized for
\mathtt{\mathit{p}}\times\mathtt{\mathit{q}}
and
\mathtt{\mathit{q}}\times\mathtt{\mathit{r}}

(if
\mathtt{\mathit{p}}
,
\mathtt{\mathit{q}}
, and
\mathtt{\mathit{r}}
are all non-negative;
an assertion failure will be raised otherwise).

To reflect the operational behavior,
code-generating functions are assigned types peculiar to staged computation.
For example,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
is assigned
type

The body of the bracket is basically given type

\mathtt{Mat}\ 4\ 5\to\mathtt{Mat}\ 2\ 3\to\mathtt{Mat}\ 1\ 3\to\mathtt{Mat}\ 4\ 3

and it is guaranteed not to cause shape mismatch (as far as it is
applied to matrices of the designated sizes). Note that no
sophisticated machinery is required if one wants to do some type-guided traversal on generated code,
possibly for further optimization; a simple type system (with infinitely many
base types
\mathtt{Mat}\ 1\ 1,\mathtt{Mat}\ 1\ 2,\mathtt{Mat}\ 2\ 1,\ldots
) suffices
5
5

5

The types of primitives are also simple.
For example,
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}_{\mathtt{2},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{3}}}
is given

\mathtt{Mat}\ 2\ 3\to\mathtt{Mat}\ 1\ 3\to\mathtt{Mat}\ 3\ 3
.

.

In this way, we can verify the consistency
during code-generating compile-time computation.
We expect that, in many cases, compile-time computation does not take much time
and that inconsistencies will be immediately detected as assertion failures.
If the stage-
0
evaluation succeeds, i.e., produces a code fragment without causing any failure,
the resulting code fragment is guaranteed to be consistent with respect to specific tensor shapes.
In this sense, we can do tensor shape checking
without relying on either manual or automated proving,
and thus mitigate the aforementioned issues A, B, and C
(We defer to Section
2.2

how the remaining issue D can be resolved in our method).
One may see this approach as a compile-time version of

manifest contracts

[
22
,
30
,
31
,
61
]
,

hybrid type checking

[
23
,
46
]
,
or some similar methods like Lemay et al.
[
47
]
.
Our approach might also be able to be seen as
some kind of staging-based foundation of
the
template metaprogramming
in C++
[
38
]
.

Nonetheless, now we have to write many “annotation-like” arguments
in exchange for the absence of proofs
(like the three arguments in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
).
Manually adding staging constructs may also be cumbersome.
In Section
2
,
we illustrate that most of these descriptions can actually be cleared away
by introducing surface languages.

1.3
Our Contributions

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

1.

Staged core language for compile-time tensor shape checking
and the mathematical guarantee of its safety
:
Based on the formalization of staged computation,
we define
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
, a two-stage language that enables us to ensure
the consistency of tensor shapes at stage-
0
(i.e., compile-time) computation.
This formalization can be considered handy for real-world use
in continuous software development
in that it requires neither manual nor automated proofs
for type-checking programs.
At the same time, our method achieves runtime safety in the sense that,

once a code fragment specialized for specific tensor shapes is generated after compile-time computation,
it is guaranteed to contain no shape mismatches and thereby can be run safely
.
Our method also accommodates
complex tensor manipulations that are frequently used in DNN-related programs,
such as
broadcasting

[
19
,
14
]

or
reshaping
.
Furthermore, our formalization incorporates
refinement types

[
23
,
58
,
46
,
33
]

so that detailed preconditions expected of stage-
0
function parameters can be described by types
for the sake of error localization.

2.

Extension with implicit arguments and their reconstruction rules
:
To alleviate the burden of specifying shape-related stage-
0
arguments,
we define
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
,
an extended version of
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
with implicit parameters/arguments,
and provide algorithmic rules for the reconstruction of omitted arguments.
Although this inference is not complete, it can reconstruct omitted arguments in many typical cases.

3.

Horsea, an example non-staged surface language
:
As an exemplification of adding a non-staged surface language on top of the staged core language,
we design
Horsea
, which frees us from
manually adding staging constructs and many shape-related arguments.
By using
binding-time analysis
(
BTA
)
[
41
,
16
,
17
]
,
programs in this surface language are translated to

\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
(and finally to
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
by reconstructing implicit arguments).

4.

Prototype implementation
:
We implemented a prototype type-checker of Horsea in Haskell based on our method
and made it publicly available
[
64
,
65
]
.
This type-checker exemplifies that our method is expressive enough to
verify the shape consistency of
10 example programs
6
6

6

Although our method seems able to cover the other remaining examples as well,
we could not port them simply due to the lack of time;
assigning appropriate types to
ocaml-torch
’s API
and understanding original programs as to unreconstructible implicit arguments
requires a bit of time and effort.

offered by
ocaml-torch

[
10
]
,
an OCaml binding of PyTorch
[
54
]
,
by porting them to Horsea manually and feed them to our type-checker.

We suppose that our method alleviates the issues A–D from the following perspectives:

A.

Since it only requires type annotations for binders and
some implicit arguments that cannot be inferred,
it would not hamper future changes to a large extent.

B.

Since compile-time computations can be
described in a usual functional language,
one can expect that users can easily estimate the elapsed time for shape checking.
Furthermore, for typical cases, the elapsed time will be quite instant (say, less than 0.1 second).

C.

Our method does not cause false positive errors about tensor shapes
in the sense that equations of tensor shapes are tested by concrete values after specializing them.

D.

As explained in Section
2.2
,
our method accommodates operations that perform implicit shape conversions such as broadcasting.

We here note that
our formalization is not something that completely replaces theorem-proving approaches;
our language ensures the shape consistency

only after
concrete tensor shapes are given
for compile-time code generation.
By contrast, for verifying the consistency of a tensor-handling library,
it is essentially necessary to prove that
the library works for
any possible combination
of tensor shapes,
but our method cannot ensure properties that cannot be judged by evaluation,
e.g., essentially universally quantified propositions.
In this sense, the target population of our language design is
end users who are implementing specific heavy tensor computations
rather than authors of tensor-handling libraries.
Nonetheless, it is possible to utilize our method for
testing
libraries
in a way like
property-based testing

[
13
]
,
i.e., by running code generation with many randomly selected combinations of tensor shapes.
Also, although in a somewhat awkward manner
and with the aid of the so-called
\mathbf{run}
-primitive
[
67
,
72
,
32
,
44
]
,
our method accommodates programs that handle
tensors whose sizes are known only at runtime;
Section
6.2
discusses how to achieve this.

Overall picture of elaboration

The rest of the paper is organized as follows:
First, Section

Section

and

Section

and gives how to infer omitted arguments.
Section

as a proof-of-concept, non-staged surface language,

2
Overview

2.1
Implicit Arguments and Their Inference

As we saw in Section
1.2
, in exchange for the absence of proofs,
programs apparently require many “annotation-like” arguments for tensor shapes.
Actually, we can infer many of such arguments even if they are omitted.
With implicit arguments, we can write
\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}
as follows:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{A}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\hskip 10.00002pt{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{D}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}=}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathbf{in}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{A}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{D}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

All the shape-related arguments applied to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}

are now implicit; they will be inferred
by using the type of already defined identifiers (such as built-in functions)
and type annotations provided by the user.

For implicit parameters/arguments, we first introduce

\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
,
a variant form of stage-
0
dependent function types.
Functions of this type work exactly the same as
those of type
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
from the operational perspective,
but they allow users to omit arguments
and require the type-checker to infer an expression that should substitute
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}

for each context.
For example,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
is now assigned
type
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
,
meaning
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}
can be implicit.
Users can also define a function with implicit arguments by using
variant
\lambda
-abstractions of the
form
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
.
In addition, when one wants to specify arguments explicitly for implicit parameters,
applications of the form
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}
can be used.

The reconstruction of implicit arguments can be done in a type-guided manner.
For example, consider the subexpression
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}
,
and let
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
, and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}
denote
expressions that should be reconstructed for the three parameters.
According to the type assigned to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
,
the reconstructed subexpression
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}

will have type

{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}
.
Since this subexpression is applied to
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}
, which has type
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
,
the domain type
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}
must be identical to
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
after evaluation.
In this case, we can infer that
it suffices to just substitute
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}
with

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
, respectively.
Similarly, by comparing
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}
with the type of
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}
(i.e.,
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
),
we can judge that
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}
can be used as
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.
We have found that this kind of reconstruction can be formalized by using
a technique adapted from Xie and Oliveira’s “
let arguments go first
”
[
76
]
;
other well-trodden approaches such as Hindley–Milner-like unification might also work,
but our formalization seems more concise (and still effective enough) in that
it suffices to track variables for substitution
only locally
.
Although the reconstruction is essentially incomplete
(i.e., even when there exist appropriate expressions,
it cannot always infer them),
our reconstuction algorithm is fairly effective for typical use cases, as we will report later.
Even when it cannot infer an argument, the algorithm can still report
the position where the user should explicitly give arguments.

2.2
Support for Implicit Tensor Conversion

As we have mentioned in the issue D,
it would be desirable to support
some implicit conversions of tensors,
such as
broadcasting

[
19
,
14
]
,
which are frequently used in DNN-related programs.
Our language can safely support the tensor addition with broadcasting
by providing a code-generating built-in function
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genAdd}}}
of the following type:

\displaystyle\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcast}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}},

where
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcast}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}

is a partial function that returns the shape to which two given shapes
can be commonly broadcastable.
Receiving two lists
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{10}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}
and
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{10}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}
, for example,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genAdd}}}
returns code
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{add}}_{[\mathtt{5},\mathtt{3},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10}],[\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{10}]}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
,
where
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{add}}_{[\mathtt{5},\mathtt{3},\mathtt{1},\mathtt{10}],[\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{10}]}}
is the specialized tensor addition
of the following type:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{10}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{10}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{10}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}.

On the other hand, if
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genAdd}}}
is applied to
two shapes that are not broadcastable to one common shape,
it will emit a failure,
just as
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
will do for negative integers.

2.3
Error Localization by Stage-0 Refinement Types

One aspect that provides a source for improving the language design is
how errors during compile-time computation are reported.
Other than casts
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T_{1}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T_{2}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}
,
stage-
0
functions may also emit a failure since some of them are partial
(e.g.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
cannot take negative integers).
Certainly, in both cases, failures can happen only at compile time
and can be reported in a somewhat human-friendly manner
since they point to a code position by
\ell
,
but the problem is that a reported position does not necessarily identify the direct source of the bug;
it can be a position inside a function that does not contain erroneous descriptions,
and the reported position should rather be one of the call sites.
For example, consider
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{-1}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}
.
This will cause an error with the position in the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}

at which
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
is applied to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}
,
i.e., the first parameter of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
.
However, it is the call site of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
passing
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{-1}}
,
not the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
,
that this error should be attributed to.
It will be better if we have a mechanism to emit a failure
when
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
is applied to a negative value like
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{-1}}
.

To this end,
we use
refinement types

[
25
,
23
,
58
,
46
]

of the form
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}

for stage-0 types.
The annotations
can be modified from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}
,
which abbreviates
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\geq}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{0}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}
:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{A}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{2}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{B}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{C}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ \ldots\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

Then, consider an application
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.
Now that the type for
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}
tracks the precondition required of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}
,
the above application elaborates to

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{\ell}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}

(assuming
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
elaborates to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
),
where
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathrm{rfn}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{\ell}
is a cast function
to assert that the argument satisfies the predicate of the refinement type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathrm{rfn}}}
,
and
\ell
is a label that points to the original application.
This will emit a failure if
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
evaluates to a negative integer
and report the position of the call site
\ell
.
Compared to the original situation where failures are raised by

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
used in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}}
,
programmers can describe more detailed preconditions expected of arguments,
and the type-checker can
point to the location where some precondition was violated.
We allow refinement types only for stage
0
, and thereby
the evaluation of such casts happens only at compile time,
i.e., runtime evaluation is still free from assertion failures.

We note that refinement types are also beneficial for
error localization as to implicit conversion;
with refinement types, we can assign
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genAdd}}}
the following more natural type:

\displaystyle\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcastable}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcast}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{y}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}},

where
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}
is a basetype for shapes that intuitively works as
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}
,
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcastable}}}
judges whether a pair of two shapes
is in the domain of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcast}}}
.
As a sideline,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcast}}}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{broadcastable}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}

is now a total function.

2.4
Horsea: A Seemingly Dependently-Typed Surface Language

Although many shape-related arguments are now inferred,
we still manually add staging constructs,
i.e., brackets
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
and escapes
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}
.
This might be inconvenient for some users,
especially those who are unfamiliar with staged computation.
As a solution to this cumbersomeness,
there are a number of ways to provide a surface language that is less explicit as to staging
and to reconstruct where to insert gaps between stages.
To provide a proof-of-concept language for the moment, we pick up

binding-time analysis
(
BTA
)
[
41
,
16
,
17
]
,
a well-known classical technique in the literature of partial evaluation.
On top of the staged language, we give a surface language named
Horsea
7
7

7

In Japanese, seahorses are called
tatsu-no-otoshi-go

(“dragon’s lost children”) due to their resemblance to Asian-style dragons.
We use the name of a seahorse character for our surface language,
reflecting the fact that programs in the language are syntactically similar to
but internally quite different from those in Idris
[
7
,
8
]
,
which was named after a dragon character.

that is sheerly non-staged (i.e., does not require manual staging at all).
In fact, users can describe
\mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}
in Horsea as follows:

\displaystyle\mathbf{let}\ \mathtt{\mathit{f^{\prime}}}\ \{\mathtt{\mathit{j}}:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{\mathtt{\mathit{k}}:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{\mathtt{\mathit{m}}:\mathtt{Nat}\}\ \{\mathtt{\mathit{n}}:\mathtt{Nat}\}

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\!\hskip 10.00002pt\ (\mathtt{\mathit{A}}:\mathtt{Mat}\ \mathtt{\mathit{j}}\ (\mathtt{\mathit{k}}+\mathtt{2}\ast\mathtt{\mathit{m}}))\ (\mathtt{\mathit{B}}:\mathtt{Mat}\ \mathtt{\mathit{m}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{n}})\ (\mathtt{\mathit{C}}:\mathtt{Mat}\ \mathtt{\mathit{k}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{n}})=

\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt\mathbf{let}\ \mathtt{\mathit{D}}=\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}\ (\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{B}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{C}})\ \mathtt{\mathit{B}}\ \mathbf{in}\ \mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{A}}\ \mathtt{\mathit{D}}

As one can see,
thanks to the omission of some stage-
0
arguments and staging constructs,
we can finally write a program that is syntactically quite similar to
the first code in the Idris-like language.
On the contrary, no
\mathbf{rewrite}
s are necessary for type equality here.

Given a program in Horsea, we perform BTA to find out
which parts can be at compile time and
insert brackets and escapes accordingly.
For this conversion, built-in functions in Horsea (e.g.,
\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}
)
are associated with those in the staged language (e.g.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}
).

3
Staged Language

In this section, we explain how our staged core language
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
is formalized.
Since
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
performs elaboration for cast insertion,
it has a source syntax and a target syntax.

3.1
Syntax, Typing Rules, and Operational Semantics

The source syntax is defined by the following
M^{(b)}
and
S^{(b)}
,
which range over the set of stage-
b
expressions and that of stage-
b
type annotations, respectively
(for
b\in\{0,1\}
):

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}c}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}s}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}B}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}

\displaystyle B

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\mathtt{Bool}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\ \mathrel{::=}\ }\hskip-10.00002pt\ \mid\ {\mathtt{Int}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\ \mathrel{::=}\ }\hskip-10.00002pt\ \mid\ {\mathtt{NatList}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\ \mathrel{::=}\ }\hskip-10.00002pt\ \mid\ {\mathtt{Float}}\ \mid\ {\cdots}

Here,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}
and
c
respectively range over
the set of built-in functions available only at stage
0
(e.g.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
)
and the set of constants usable at both stages,
which includes base constants (e.g.,
\mathtt{42}
or
\mathtt{true}
) and
stage-agnostic built-in functions (e.g.,
+
or
\mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}_{\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{5}}
).
While the application of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}
may be restricted by refinement predicates
(e.g., one cannot pass
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{-1}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
),

c
must be simply-typed.
Each constant ranged over by
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}
or
c
has its own arity,
and in particular, base constants are stage-agnostic constants of arity
0
.
We denote these arities by
\mathop{\mathrm{ar}}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p})
and
\mathop{\mathrm{ar}}(c)
.
To report the cause of compile-time assertion failures,
each occurrence of function application is equipped with a unique label
\ell

that points to its code position.
Users do not have to write these labels; they are simply attached by a pre-processor.

The most essential part of the syntax is that

1
tensor types
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

have a stage-
0
expression

of type

to represent a tensor shape
8
8

8

While
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}
is just a shorthand for
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\geq}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{0}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{NatList}}
is a base type.
This will simplify metatheory.

.
This gap between tensor types and their argument expressions as to stages
ensures, for example, that
all the stage-

\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ \ldots\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}

will be
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}[}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}]}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ \ldots\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}
after compile-time computation
and thereby that every tensor in generated code has a specialized shape.
Stage-

By contrast, stage-

In response to the setting of stage-

Stage-
0
assertions have two forms.
The first one is
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}
,
which judges that the stage-
1
types
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}

syntactically coincide after evaluation.
Interestingly, adding assertions of this form covers
all the necessary cases for checking type equality itself.
The attachment
L
stands for the source of errors when the assertion fails.
The other one
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}
is used for checking the validity of downcasts.
In operational terms,
it basically works as an identity function, but before returning the argument (say
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}
) as is,
it checks whether the argument satisfies the predicate
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
,
i.e., whether
[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}/{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}]{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
evaluates to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{true}}
.
The variant
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}
called an
active check
is
the intermediate form of this assertion process,
where
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
is a “refinement proposition”
(i.e., the application of the refinement predicate
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
to the tested value
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}
)
under evaluation.
It also keeps
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}
separately so that it will evaluate to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}
when the assertion passes.
Only the first one of these two assertion forms is new;
the latter device is ported from the context of
manifest contracts
[
30
,
61
]
.

ST1-Tensor

Figure 2:
Source typing rules with assertion insertion

Typing judgments are defined as
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}M^{(b)}:T^{(b)}\rightsquigarrow N^{(b)}
(for
b\in\{0,1\}
),
which can be read as “under the type environment
\mathit{\Gamma}
,
the source expression
M^{(b)}
has type
T^{(b)}

and elaborates to
N^{(b)}
by assertion insertion.”
The structure of type environments are defined by:

\mathit{\Gamma}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\bullet}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Gamma},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}:({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})^{0}}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Gamma},{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}:({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1}}
,
i.e,
\mathit{\Gamma}
tracks the stage at which each variable was bound.
Figure
2
shows the typing rules for these judgments.
The rules
S0-Brkt
and
S1-Esc
are peculiar to staged computation
and are natural extensions from the literature.

S0-Abs
and
S1-Abs
elaborate the type annotations
by using the judgments
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}S^{(b)}\rightsquigarrow T^{(b)}
.
Also, for constants, we have
S0-Cst0
,
S0-CstP
, and
S1-CstP
.
Here, we use two environments
\mathcal{B}_{0}
and
\mathcal{B}_{\%}
;
the former maps stage-
0
-specific built-in functions
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}

to stage-
0
types
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
,
and the latter works similarly for stage-agnostic constants
c
.
The metavariable
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
and its
unlifting

\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

will be introduced shortly.
Entries are like the following:

\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{0}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}})=\begin{aligned} &\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{r}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\\

I-Arr

Figure 3:
The rules for type compatibility and cast term generation

The most distinctive typing rules are those for applications,
i.e.,
S0-App
and
S1-App
.
Here,
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathrel{||}^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
judges
type compatibility
, i.e.,
type equivalence ignoring the difference of argument expressions,
and
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash_{L}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\triangleleft{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}
generates
assertive cast terms

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}
.
Figure
3
displays the rules for these judgments.
Among these rules,
I-Code
is the core of the cast term generation;
it checks the compatibility of given two types
and simply produces an “atomic” cast term
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}
.

I-Arr
, which works for functions, is another characteristic rule.
It produces two cast terms for domain types and codomain types, respectively,
and combines them.
Thanks to this rule, we can handle higher-order programs without any hindrance.
This mechanism is partially inspired by
GraTen
[
33
]

and
\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{H}}^{\sigma}

[
61
]
.
