ET1-Arr1

Figure 4:
Reduction relations
(selective; see Figures
11

and
12
for full definition)

Assertive terms are equipped with
staged call-by-value small-step reduction relations

N^{(b)}\longrightarrow^{b}(N^{\prime(b)}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\Uparrow}^{L})

defined in a straightforward manner except that
(1) argument expressions in assertions are evaluated,
and for this purpose, type expressions in the programs are evaluated as well as terms;
(2) when an assertion for type equality passes, it evaluates to an identity function; and that
(3) when assertion fails, it evaluates to a special symbol
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\Uparrow}^{L}
standing for failures,
and then the result
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\Uparrow}^{L}
is propagated to the whole program.
Figure
4
displays the rules for this operational semantics,
where stage-
b
values
v^{(b)}
(for
b\in\{0,1\}
)
and
stage-
1
type values

{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
are defined by the following:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}c}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}\hskip 20.00003pt{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}B}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}s}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}

Intuitively,
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
correspond to
“completed” code fragments and type annotations, respectively.
Here,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}
ranges over the set of
runtime constants
, which consists of
base constants and possibly partially applied built-in functions
(e.g.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
or
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}
).
More formally,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}
ranges over the following:
(i)
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}
with
\mathop{\mathrm{ar}}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c})=0
(i.e., base constants),
(ii)
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ \cdots\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
such that
k<\mathop{\mathrm{ar}}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p})
,
and (iii)
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ \cdots\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
such that
k<\mathop{\mathrm{ar}}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c})
.
Note that, unlike stage-
1
type expressions,
we do not have to evaluate stage-
0
type expressions;
while stage-
1
types should remain in produced code
(possibly for further post-process optimization),
stage-
0
types are all thrown away by
\beta
-reduction
through stage-
0
computation.

To deal with applications of built-in functions,

E0-Delta
uses
the so-called delta reduction
\delta
,
which maps a pair consisting of an operation and a complete array of operands to
a value of the form
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}q}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}c}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}}
.
Entries of
\delta
are like the following:

\displaystyle\delta(+,({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{42}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{57}}))={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{99}},\hskip 20.00003pt\delta({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}},({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}))=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}_{\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{5}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}.

As an abuse of notations, we often write

\delta({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c})
for
\delta({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\hat{c}},({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}))

(resp.
\delta({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p},({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}},\ldots,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}))
)
when
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\hat{c}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ \cdots\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
(resp.
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}a}=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ \cdots\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c_{\mathit{k}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
).

When code generation successfully terminates with a code value
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
,
such
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
can be regarded as a stage-
0
term by

unlifting
operations
\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
and
\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
:

\displaystyle\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}):={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\hskip 20.00003pt\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}):={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ \mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})\hskip 20.00003pt\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}):=\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}})\ \mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}})

\displaystyle\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}c}):={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}c}\hskip 20.00003pt\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}s}):={\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}s}\hskip 20.00003pt\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}B}):=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\nu}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mid}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{true}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}

\displaystyle\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}):=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}})\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}})\hskip 10.00002pt\text{(where ${\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\not\in\mathop{\mathrm{fv}}(\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}))$)}

One can then evaluate
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:=\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})
as ordinary runtime execution,
which will not cause any failure since
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
contains no assertions.

Lastly, we note that, while reduction rules make sense to open terms as well,
we suppose that only closed terms can step,
i.e., all the reduction rules implicitly require that the reduced term be closed.
Here, by closed terms, we mean those in which no
stage-0
variables freely occur;
stage-1 variables are not considered,
and hence
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{1}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
is a closed term, for example.
This restriction is crucial for our metatheory,
specifically for proving
cotermination

[
61
]
.

T1-Var

Figure 5:
Target typing for metatheory

For the purpose of proving type safety, assertive terms are also assigned types
by declarative target typing of the form
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}N^{(b)}:T^{(b)}
.
Figure
5
displays the rules for these judgments.
Some of the rules depend on type equivalences
T^{(b)}_{1}\equiv^{b}T^{(b)}_{2}

and well-formedness judgments
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}T^{(b)}
and
\vdash\mathit{\Gamma}

defined respectively in Figures
13
and
14
in Appendix.
The equivalences
\equiv^{b}
are necessarily introduced
to prove Preservation as to function applications.

We first prove that well-typed source terms are always elaborated to
assertive terms well-typed under target typing,
by relatively straightforward induction:

Theorem 1

(Soundness of Assertion Insertion)
.

If
\vdash\mathit{\Gamma}
and
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}M^{(b)}:T^{(b)}\rightsquigarrow N^{(b)}
,
then
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}N^{(b)}:T^{(b)}
.

Proving Preservation and Progress
[
56
]
is much more challenging
due to the combination of the
\delta
-reduction, the type equivalences
\equiv^{b}
,
and the dependent nature of our typing.
To prove Preservation as to built-in functions,
we must assume some natural properties on
\mathcal{B}_{0}
,
\mathcal{B}_{\%}
, and
\delta
.
For example, since

\delta({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}},({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}))=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}_{\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{5}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

holds,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVertCat}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{3}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{4}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{5}}
and
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vertCat}}_{\mathtt{3},\mathtt{4},\mathtt{5}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

must have equivalent types.
However, we cannot use the type equivalences to describe such assumptions;
because the definition of equivalences will depend on
\delta
,
we have to avoid the dependency of the reverse direction
in order not to make the validity circular.
To this end, we have to use reduction relations, rather than equivalences.
We put the resulting descriptions as Assumption
8
in Appendix
because they are one-page long.

Another challenging point arising after identifying the above assumptions is
how to define the type equivalences
\equiv^{b}
precisely.
They must be at least compatible with the
\beta
-equivalence,
but the
\beta
-equivalence itself is actually too loose;
in order to prove Preservation as to
\delta
,
we must define
\equiv^{b}
carefully so that
they preserve the “reducibility” of refinement predicates to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{true}}
.
For this purpose, following Sekiyama et al.
[
61
]
,
we can extend and use the
common subexpression reduction
(
CSR
) equivalence
[
31
,
61
]
,
which is the equivalence spanned by the relation that allows
the usual call-by-value reduction for arbitrary
closed
subexpressions.

Under these settings,
we have proved the following safety properties,
where
\vdash^{1}\mathit{\Gamma}
means that all the entries in
\mathit{\Gamma}
are of the form

({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}:({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1})
:

Theorem 2

(Preservation)
.

If
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}N^{(b)}:T^{(b)}
and
N^{(b)}\longrightarrow^{b}N^{\prime(b)}
,
then
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}N^{\prime(b)}:T^{(b)}
.

Theorem 3

(Progress)
.

If
\vdash^{1}\mathit{\Gamma}
and
\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{b}N^{(b)}:T^{(b)}
, then we have one of the following:
(1)
N^{(b)}\longrightarrow^{b}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\Uparrow}^{L}
;
(2) there exists
N^{\prime(b)}
such that
N^{(b)}\longrightarrow^{b}N^{\prime(b)}
; or
(3)
N^{(b)}
is a value.

Lemma 5
.

{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\equiv^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
implies
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}={\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.

We prove this by separating it into two:
(1)
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\equiv^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
implies
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\cong^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
,
where
\cong^{b}
is the standard
\beta
-equivalence; and
(2)
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\cong^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
implies
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}={\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.
While the former is straightforward, the latter requires slight attention:
the reduction includes the rule
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}\longrightarrow^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
,
which is not left-linear in the sense that
the metavariable
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
appears more than once on the left-hand side.
In such a reduction system, confluence is often hard to show or even broken.
Nonetheless, in our cases,
it turns out to be sufficient to use a standard syntactic approach to consistency,
which defines parallel reduction corresponding to the equivalence and prove
the uniqueness of normal forms via confluence.
Thanks to Lemma
5
,
we can finally prove Lemma
4
.

Since unlifted code does not contain

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}p}
or assertions and is typeable without the type equivalences,
the combination of the theorems and lemmata above ensures that,
if the source program elaborates to a term and
the term evaluates to a code value without failures,
we will not have runtime shape mismatches when running the produced code:

Corollary 7
.

If
\bullet\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

,
then
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}
is of the form
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
, and
this
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
satisfies one of the following:

such that

, or
(2) the evaluation of
\mathop{\downarrow}({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}v^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})
does not halt
9
9

9

More precisely, unless extended with recursive functions,

\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
is strongly normalizing,
and thus (2) does not happen.

.

4
Implicit Arguments and Their Inference

To alleviate the burden of manually adding
shape-related stage-
0
arguments in
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
,
we offer
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}

an extension of
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}

as mentioned in Section

.
This section formalizes

and explains how to infer implicit arguments.

First, the source syntax is

\lambda
-abstractions and applications
10
10

10

Some contexts will newly allow

-abstractions without a type annotation

This is closely related to how the reconstruction algorithm is designed;

-abstractions.

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}B}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathcal{S}^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathcal{S}^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}

The construct
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{S}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
works as

\lambda
-abstractions whose parameter can be implicit,
and
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}_{\ell}
can be used to specify an argument for such parameters explicitly.
The form
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\_}
lies between complete omission and explicit designation;
it indicates the existence of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
’s implicit parameter,
but does not specify a concrete expression for it.
This is useful, e.g., for specifying an argument for only the second implicit parameter
by
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\_}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}_{\ell}
.

As mentioned earlier in Section
2.1
,
we reconstruct implicit arguments through type-checking
as well as inserting compile-time assertions.
This process can be formalized by utilizing
“
let arguments go first
”
[
76
]
,
which is a variant of
bidirectional type-checking

[
55
,
21
]
;
when checking applications, we first traverse the argument to obtain its type
and then inspect the function, not the other way around as usual.
To handle dependent function types and cast insertion,
our formalization extends Xie and Oliveira’s original work
in several aspects, such as the form of
application contexts
and return types,
which will be explained below.

BT0-Imp

Figure 7:
Rules for inferring implicit arguments
(selective; see Figures
15

and
16
for full definition)

Figure
7
displays the rules for
the new elaboration that simultaneously performs type-checking,
assertion insertion, and the reconstruction of implicit arguments.
The main judgments for stage-
b
expressions are

\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{b}\mathcal{M}^{(b)}\Rightarrow R^{(b)}\rightsquigarrow N^{(b)}

(for
b\in\{0,1\}
), which can be understood as
“under the type environment
\mathcal{G}
and the
application context

\mathit{\Psi}
,
the expression
\mathcal{M}^{(b)}
is well-typed and can be elaborated to the target term
N^{(b)}
,
and its type is
instantiated
to
R^{(b)}
at this context.”
A number of new devices are introduced for this elaboration,
so we will explain them one by one.
First, as can be seen from the judgments,
the syntax of target terms remains the same as
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)}
; we keep using
N^{(b)}
.
Type environments
\mathcal{G}
used here are normal entities
that just associate stage-
b
variables with stage-
b
types for
b\in\{0,1\}
, respectively:

\mathcal{G}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\bullet}\ \mid\ {\mathcal{G},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}:({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})^{0}}\ \mid\ {\mathcal{G},{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}x}:({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1}}
.
The sole notable thing is that, while we continue using
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
for stage-
1
types,
the syntax of stage-
0
types is extended with those for functions with implicit parameters as follows:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}B}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Tensor}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}s}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}}

Some rules in Figure
7
uses the evident injection
\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\rfloor

of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
-types to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
-types, which simply forgets the difference between

\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
and
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.

One of the essential devices to do “let arguments go first” is

application contexts

\mathit{\Psi}
.
When checking an expression
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
that is expected to be a function,
the stack
\mathit{\Psi}
provides information about the outside,
i.e., what kind of sequence is passed as arguments of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
:

\displaystyle\mathit{\Psi}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\bullet}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Psi},({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})^{0}_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Psi},\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Psi},\__{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\mathit{\Psi},({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1}_{\ell}}

An entry
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})^{0}_{\ell}
(resp.
\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}^{0}_{\ell}
)
stands for the existence of a stage-
0
mandatory argument
(resp. an explicitly specified argument for an implicit parameter)
of type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
whose elaboration result is
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.
Unlike the original work
[
76
]
,
we push actual arguments to
\mathit{\Psi}
as well as the types of the arguments
to instantiate the type of the function applied to them, as explained later.
The other two forms can be understood in the same way;

\__{\ell}
and
({\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1}_{\ell}

represents the existence of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\_}
and a stage-
1
argument of type
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
, respectively.
The rules
B0-App
,
B0-AppImp
,
B0-FillImp
, and
B1-App

appropriately push these entries to the stack
\mathit{\Psi}

to check the function after traversing the argument first.
The stacked entries will be popped by some rules, such as

B0-Var
or
B1-Var
.

B0-Var
instantiates the type of the variable
guided by
\mathit{\Psi}

by using an auxiliary judgment
\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.
This instantiates
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
to an
extended return type

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

so that the domain types can match the types of the arguments passed to the variable.

B1-Var
and
\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
do basically the same thing
for stage-
1
variables.
The syntax of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
is defined by the following:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {D\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}}

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {D\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}\ \mid\ {{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}}

\displaystyle D

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ /\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})^{0}}\ \mid\ {\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ /\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}}\ \mid\ {({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ /\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}})^{1}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\ \mathrel{::=}\ }\hskip-10.00002pt\ \mid\ {\mathbf{fill}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}}\ \mid\ {\mathbf{insert}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}}

As the name suggests, extended return types basically work as types;

D\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
can be seen as a function type
just by regarding the
extended domain

D
as
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
or
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.
The difference from usual types is that extended domains are
equipped with a cast term or a reconstructed term that works as
a “feedback” for the corresponding application site.

B0-App
inserts into the elaborated application
the cast term
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}
returned by the traversal of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
,
and
B0-FillImp
compensates for the hole
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\_}
with the inferred term
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.

B0-InsertImp
works basically the same as
B0-FillImp
,
but it inserts the inferred term
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
rather than filling
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\_}
.
Some other rules also use terms conveyed by extended domains for elaboration.
One can easily see that the shape of
R^{(b)}
is determined
basically in response to
\mathit{\Psi}
in each rule.

Due to the existence of
B0-InsertImp
,
one may think that
typing derivation is not syntax-directed and thereby uninterpretable as an algorithm.
However,

\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\Rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
can actually be read as an algorithm in the following ways,
where
(\mathcal{G},\mathit{\Psi},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})
and
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}})
are regarded as inputs and outputs, respectively:
Suppose that, during the check of an expression
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
,
the traversal of a subexpression
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}
returned
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}})
.

(i)

If
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}
is of the form
\mathbf{insert}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
,
then, the sole possible rule used directly below is
B0-InsertImp
,
and one can thereby replace the output with
({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}},\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}})
.

(ii)

Repeat the process (i) until
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}
is no longer of the form
\mathbf{insert}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.
Then, one can use the rule corresponding to the form of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.

That is, in a broad sense, typing rules are syntax-directed
with respect to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

and all the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
’s produced by its subexpressions
,
not just to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{M}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
.

\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\lfloor\mathcal{G}\rfloor\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rfloor\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}/{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}]{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi},\__{\ell}\vdash^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}\mathbf{fill}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}

BI0-ImpGuess1

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\text{$\mathit{\Psi}$ is neither of the form~$(\mathit{\Psi}^{\prime},\__{\ell})$ nor $(\mathit{\Psi}^{\prime},\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\}_{\ell})$}\\
\lfloor\mathcal{G}\rfloor\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rfloor\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}/{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}]{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}\mathbf{insert}\ \{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\lfloor\mathcal{G}\rfloor\vdash_{\ell}\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rfloor\triangleleft\lfloor{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rfloor\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}/{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}]{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi},\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\}_{\ell}\vdash^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{<:}\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ /\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}

BI1-Arr

Figure 8:
The declarative rules for the inference of implicit arguments

The core of our inference lies in
the judgments
\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}
and
\mathcal{G}\mid\mathit{\Psi}\vdash^{1}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}\mathrel{<:}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}R^{\scriptscriptstyle(1)}}
.
Figure
8
first shows
the declarative rules for these judgments.
Guided by the application context,
BI0-Arr
and
BI0-ImpGiven

instantiate the codomain type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}

by substituting
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}
with
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
,
i.e., the given argument wrapped by an appropriate cast function.

BI0-ImpGuess
guesses an implicit argument
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}
;
for actual implementation, we have to infer it algorithmically.
The intuition for defining an algorithmic version is quite simple:
we can track a finite set
I
of variables
that should be resolved into a term through the traversal, and
if about to insert casts for a type
that contains unresolved variables and has some suitable structure,
we can simply interpret that equation as a solution.
For space reasons, the algorithmic rules are described
in Figure
17
in Appendix.
We mention only the most important one:
ABI0-ImpGuess
.
It adds
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}
to
I
as unresolved
and extracts the solution for
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}
from the substitution
\theta_{{\mathrm{2}}}

after traversing
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathcal{T}^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}
.
If
\theta_{{\mathrm{2}}}
does not contain
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}x}
,
it means that the inference failed;
in this case, the type-checker will emit an error with the label
\ell
.

5
Basics of Horsea

To lessen the cumbersomeness of manually inserting staging constructs,
we provide a proof-of-concept surface language named
Horsea
.
Programs in this language are translated into

\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
by reconstructing staging constructs.
This section explains the basics of
how to properly complement
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}
.
The reconstruction process is formalized as an elaboration through type-checking-like traversal.
The target language of the elaboration is
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
,
which we have introduced in Section
4
.
The formalization is fairly standard;
we can reconstruct
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}

by a well-known technique in the literature of partial evaluation
called
binding-time analysis
(
BTA
)
[
41
,
16
,
17
]
.
Because most part of the formalization is simply a repetition of classical results,
precise descriptions are deferred to Appendix
C
.
Nonetheless, care must be taken to handle dependent function types and implicit arguments in our case.

The syntax of source expressions
E
and type annotations
T

is quite concise:

\displaystyle E

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {d}\ \mid\ {x}\ \mid\ {\lambda x:T.\ E}\ \mid\ {(E_{{\mathrm{1}}}\ E_{{\mathrm{2}}})_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\lambda\{x:T\}.\ E}\ \mid\ {(E_{{\mathrm{1}}}\ \{E_{{\mathrm{2}}}\})_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {E\ \_}

\displaystyle T

\displaystyle\ \mathrel{::=}\ {B}\ \mid\ {\{x:B\mid E\}}\ \mid\ {\mathtt{Tensor}\ E}\ \mid\ {(x:T)\to T}

As one can see, this is basically “
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
without staging constructs”.
Here,
d
ranges over the set of constants (e.g.,
\mathtt{\mathit{matMult}}
)
associated with corresponding ones
in
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
(e.g.,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genMatMult}}}
).

BTA assigns a
binding time

b

to every subexpression to produce
\hat{e}
defined below:

\displaystyle\hat{e}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {e^{b}}\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 10.00002pte\ \mathrel{::=}\ {d}\ \mid\ {x}\ \mid\ {\lambda x:\hat{\tau}.\ \hat{e}}\ \mid\ {(\hat{e}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\ \hat{e}_{{\mathrm{2}}})_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\lambda\{x:\hat{\tau}\}.\ \hat{e}}\ \mid\ {(\hat{e}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\ \{\hat{e}_{{\mathrm{2}}}\})_{\ell}}\ \mid\ {\hat{e}\ \_}

\displaystyle\hat{\tau}\ \mathrel{::=}\ {\tau^{b}}\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 10.00002pt\tau\ \mathrel{::=}\ {B}\ \mid\ {\mathtt{Tensor}\ \hat{e}}\ \mid\ {(x:\hat{\tau})\to\hat{\tau}}\hskip 20.00003pt\hskip 10.00002ptb\ \mathrel{::=}\ {0}\ \mid\ {1}

By the binding times (
\approx
stages) assigned to subexpressions,
we can evidently reconstruct
brackets
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
and escapes
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}

by inserting them at each gap of the two binding times on the syntax tree,
as described in Figure
21
in Appendix.
The assignment can be done by extracting binding-time constraints from programs and solving them.
For example, if the given non-staged program contains a subexpression

(\lambda\mathtt{\mathit{x}}:\mathtt{Mat}\ \mathtt{\mathit{m}}\ (\mathtt{\mathit{n}}+\mathtt{1}).\ \ldots)
, then we can extract the information that
variables
\mathtt{\mathit{m}}
and
\mathtt{\mathit{n}}
must be bound at stage
0
and
that the type annotation
\mathtt{Mat}\ \mathtt{\mathit{m}}\ (\mathtt{\mathit{n}}+\mathtt{1})
must live in stage
1
,
in order to appropriately transform the program into the staged core language.
Such constraints can be extracted in a type-checking-like manner,
as explained in Appendix
C
.

6
Further Discussions

Although the formalization we have given so far basically satisfies our goal,
we still have room for improvement for real-world use.
This section briefly touch on some of such aspects.

6.1
Adding Conditionals Is Unexpectedly Non-Trivial But Viable

In addition to the constructs in our formalization,
recursive functions and conditionals are desiderata for real-world use.
While adding the former does not incur much difficulty as to typing,
designing a rule for stage-
0

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}
-expressions is
actually not as straightforward as expected.
One may imagine that something like the following
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}
-biased rule would work:

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Bool}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}\ \text{(for $i\in\{1,2\}$)}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash_{\ell}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\triangleleft{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}^{\ell}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\end{array}}

However, this is not the actual way we want to check conditionals;
for example, it cannot handle programs like the following:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{rec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genRep}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{v}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\leq}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{0}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vecNil}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVecCat}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\{}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}-}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{v}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genRep}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}-}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{v}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

Here,
{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{vecNil}}}
is a built-in constant for the vector of length
0
,
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genVecCat}}}
is the one that produces code of vector concatenation functions.
The application
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genRep}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
produces code of a function
that takes a vector of length
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}
and duplicate it
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
times
to make the vector of length
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}
.
Because the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}
-branch and the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}
-branch
have type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{0}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}:=\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}-}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{1}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
, respectively,
the inserted assertion
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(\!\!\!\;|}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\triangleleft}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|\!)}}^{L}

will pass only when either
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}
or
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}
equals
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{0}}
.
This is clearly different from the intention;
what we wanted to assert here is that both branches have type
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.

This can be resolved by some rule that “merges” two types by conditionals as follows:

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Bool}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{\mathit{i}}}\ \text{(for $i\in\{1,2\}$)}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\begin{aligned} \mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}^{\ell}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Vec}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\prime\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\hskip 18.49988pt&\\
\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{if}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{then}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{else}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}&\end{aligned}\end{array}}

Such merging can be generalized to arbitrary compatible pairs of types.

6.2
Handling Tensors with “Essentially Dynamic” Shapes

As we have seen so far, our language is basically designed so that all the computations
will be specialized to certain tensor shapes at compile time.
However, sometimes one wants programs to deal with tensors
whose shapes are essentially unknown at compile time and available only at runtime.
Indeed, it would be quite common, for example, to set up a server-side application
that can receive image files (
\approx
matrices) of arbitrary sizes by request from users
to perform some computation on them using tensors.
To this end, with the aid of the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
-primitive
[
67
,
72
,
32
,
44
]
,
our language can also handle tensors with essentially dynamic shapes to some extent
within its design principle.
This is not completely free from runtime size mismatch,
but even if a failure happens, it will be emitted immediately,
not during actual tensor computation,
and thus the user can still avoid wasting time.

The
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
-primitive is a special construct
that can unlift code fragments like the following:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{g}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{c}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{c}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{in}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{g}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{42}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{57}}

\displaystyle\longrightarrow^{0\,\ast}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}+}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{42}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{57}}\longrightarrow^{0}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{x}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{42}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{57}}\longrightarrow^{0\,\ast}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{99}}

Note that, in general, adding
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
could require ingenious modification to the type system.
This is because one cannot always unlift code fragments;
even if the program is well-typed under naïve typing for staging,
variables occurring in code fragments passed to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
might be locally unbound
11
11

11

For example, the following term gets stuck:

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{h}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{t}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Bool}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{0}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{in}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\lambda}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{b}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}:}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Bool}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}.}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{h}}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{\mathit{b}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.

.
However, this can basically be solved by a method orthogonal to ours,
and also, as explained later, we do not have to care too much about this in our setting.

The basic idea to achieve the dynamic feature by using
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
is quite easy:
when receiving some form of a tensor whose shape has not been fixed at compile time,
we can (1) generate code of the necessary function specialized for its shape,
(2) lift the tensor to the upper stage and embed it as an argument of the produced function,
and (3) run the code to compute the final result.
An implementation for doing this would be something like the following:

\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{let}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{handle}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{out}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{FilePath}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{dynMat}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}=}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{match}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{rectSize}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{dynMat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{with}}

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{None}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{printError}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\text{{``The given matrix is not rectangular''}}}

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Some}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}m}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{match}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{forgetSize}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}m}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{genF}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}m}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\sim}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{liftMat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}m}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}n}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{dynMat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\rangle}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{with}}

\displaystyle\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Error}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{msg}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{printError}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\text{{``Bug: ''}}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}+\!+}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{msg}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\hskip 9.24994pt{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}|}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Ok}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{result}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{writeMatrixToFile}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{out}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathit{result}}

The function
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{rectSize}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Option}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathbin{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\ast}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}

first takes a dynamic matrix
and returns its size
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{m}}}\mathpunct{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8},}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{n}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}

wrapped by
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Some}}
if it is rectangular
(or returns
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{None}}
otherwise).
Then, by using this size,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genF}}}
produces code of the function necessary for the user’s purpose,
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{liftMat}}}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

lifts the matrix to code.
As an example, we here suppose the case where the function produced by
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genSomeFun}}}
returns
a matrix of the transposed size, so the type of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genSomeFun}}}
is

\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{q}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{p}}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.
After the main computation, we use

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{forgetSize}}}:\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}(}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}:}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{Nat}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8})}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\to}}\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Mat}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{j}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\%}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{k}}}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\to}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{List}}\ \mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}(}}{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{List}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0}\mathtt{Int}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0.7,0.3,0})}}\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}

so that the size of the matrix will be discarded from the type.
Finally, by using
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
, we run the code constructed so far.
Here,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
wraps resulting values with a sum type equivalent to OCaml’s
\mathtt{result}
,
and it will return an error message if some shape mismatch or unlifting failure has happened.
Namely, we cannot perfectly eliminate the possibility of runtime shape mismatch after all,
but the important point here is that,
even if the implementation of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathtt{\mathit{genSomeFun}}}
causes a shape mismatch for the given size
(or the occurrence of locally unbound variables),

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{run}}
emit errors
immediately
for typical cases;
such errors happen during code generation or unlifting, not during heavy computation involving tensors.
Thus, owing to staging,
one can still successfully avoid wasting time even if the program contains some shape mismatch.

7
Implementation Report

Based on the formalization we have given so far,
we implemented a prototype type-checker in Haskell
and made it publicly available
[
64
,
65
]
.
This type-checker accepts
both programs in
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
and those in Horsea;
when receiving a program in Horsea,
the type-checker internally converts it to the one
in
\lambda^{\langle\rangle(\!\!\!\;||\!\!\!\;)\{\}}
in a manner
explained in Section
5
.

To support realistic examples,
the type-checker extends various aspects of the languages,
such as some of the features mentioned in Section
6
.
Specifically, to handle example programs of
ocaml-torch

[
10
]
,
an OCaml binding of PyTorch
[
54
]
,
we utilize stage-
0
refinement types
to express
broadcasting

[
19
,
14
]

of tensors.
Broadcasting is a kind of implicit conversion of tensors,
and the use of refinement types for this purpose is
largely inspired by GraTen
[
33
]
.

Our aims for implementing this are the following:
(1) Because our method relies on the observation that
tensor shapes are “not very dynamic”
(i.e., that typical programs contain a limited number of operations
where the resulting shape can be determined only at runtime),
it is unclear whether our method sufficiently accommodates realistic programs.
By porting examples offered by
ocaml-torch

[
10
]

into our language, we substantiate the applicability of our method.
(2) We demonstrate that our inference algorithm can reconstruct
sufficiently many implicit arguments for the ported example programs.
(3) While the core language is proven to be type-safe,
its extension with implicit arguments and the surface language
have yet to establish a mathematical guarantee
(although they are heavily inspired by existing methods that fulfill type safety).
By feeding various programs to the type-checker,
we exemplify that the extensions indeed work fine.

Figure
9

displays the declaration of some built-in values,
where
\texttt{val}\ \texttt{\textasciitilde}x\ \ldots

and
\texttt{val}\ x\ \ldots
bind
x
at stage
0
and
1
, respectively,
and
\texttt{\&(}\cdots\texttt{)}
denotes a bracket
\mathopen{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\langle}}\cdots\mathclose{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\rangle}}
.
Here,
(M\texttt{ as }T)
is a construct for manually inserting assertions,
i.e., works like the following
12
12

12

The actual implementation as to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{as}}
-expressions
is, however, somewhat different from the rule shown here.
It is rather something that enforces
the so-called
checking mode
of bidirectional type-checking
[
21
]
.

:

\displaystyle\frac{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\hskip 18.49988pt\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash_{\ell}{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\triangleleft{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\end{array}}{\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\mathit{\Gamma}\vdash^{0}({\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}M^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}\mathbf{as}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}S^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}})^{\ell}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}T^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}\rightsquigarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{0}}}}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4,0.8}N^{\scriptscriptstyle(0)}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}\end{array}}

The function
broadcast
takes two tensor shapes,
and, if the two shapes are compatible
(i.e., if tensors of the two shapes can be injected to one common shape),
it returns that common shape, or raises a failure otherwise.
Although having
broadcast
suffices for expressing broadcasting,
expecting better error localization, we also provide
broadcastable
,
a function that judges whether given two shapes are compatible,
and use it in refinement predicates.

Figure
10
shows
an example program
mnist/linear.hrs
in Horsea,
which is ported from an example program
mnist/linear.ml

offered by
ocaml-torch

[
10
]
.
This program tries linear regression for the well-known MNIST dataset
[
18
]
.
Built-in functions used in this example are mapped to those of the core language like the following:

\displaystyle{\small\texttt{Tensor.(+)}}\mapsto{\small\texttt{Tensor.gen\_add}},\hskip 20.00003pt{\small\texttt{Tensor.mm}}\mapsto{\small\texttt{Tensor.gen\_mm}},

\displaystyle{\small\texttt{Tensor.cross\_entropy\_for\_logits}}\mapsto{\small\texttt{Tensor.gen\_cross\_entropy\_for\_logits}},\hskip 20.00003pt\ldots

Interestingly, the type-checker successfully reconstructs all the 20 implicit arguments in this program;
several functions, such as
+
and
mm
, have implicit parameters,
and our inference algorithm can compensate all of them,
in combination with the interface of modules such as
MnistHelper
.
Compared to the original program in OCaml,
the essential differences are only three annotations highlighted by
a
bold blue
typeface;
simply adding these three suffices for tensor shape checking for this case.
The first two are direct annotations for tensor shapes,
and the last one,
lift_int
, is
an annotation for BTA that turns compile-time integers into ones available at runtime as well.

mnist/linear.hrs
).
The columns “total” and “inferred” display
the total number of implicit arguments in each program and
the number of successfully inferred ones among those arguments, respectively.
Those that cannot be inferred are manually specified in the programs
(e.g.,
char_rnn/char_rnn.hrs
contains
39-37=2
manually specified implicit arguments,
and the other 37 are appropriately reconstructed by the type-checker).
We also show the number of shape-related descriptions
contained in type annotations in each program on the column “#annot”
because adding these descriptions often helps the inference.

As shown by these results, the inference algorithm works unexpectedly effective,
despite its (intentionally) plain strategy;
it can reconstruct approximately 90% of the implicit arguments.
The major source of the inference failure is, on the other hand, the use of higher-order functions.
It would thus be even better if we use Hindley–Milner-like unification-based algorithm.
It might also be beneficial for the inference to compute function applications in types
that are known to be pure and halting, such as those of
broadcast
, during type-checking.
